reply:
No. MITM is still possible because you're accepting any certificate from whoever answers at that IP.

Here's the distinction: encryption prevents *eavesdropping*. Certificate validation prevents *MITM*. They're different threats. With `rejectUnauthorized: false`, an attacker who can intercept the connection (via DNS hijacking, ARP spoofing, routing compromise, or network position) presents their own cert. Your client accepts it. Now the attacker decrypts your traffic with their private key, reads it (payment tokens, card data, transaction amounts), optionally modifies it, and re-encrypts to the real server. Silent compromise. The hardcoded URL doesn't matter—DNS or routing can be hijacked.

The cost: payment credentials exposed, transaction data readable, modifications undetected.

Fix the cert chain. If you can't, the API is misconfigured and shouldn't be in production.

grade.note: Reply correctly distinguishes encryption from authentication and explains the MITM mechanism (DNS/ARP/routing hijack) countering the hardcoded-URL claim.
